sections.note: Intro to Spacecraft Systems and Missions (1hr) is a lecture-based course to introduce students to the general concepts of space mission objectives & considerations, the space environment, and spacecraft mission subsystems. Students are encouraged to take AE 199 concurrently with AE 298 Intro to Nanosatellite Design for more application-based content. If students take AE 199 without AE 298, they will need instructor approval in order to register for ENG 491.
sections.title: Intro to Nanosatellite Seminar

sections.note: This section is for student leaders working as technical or project leads for various rocketry based student organization teams. Instructor approval required for registration.
sections.title: Rocket Dev, Safety, and Leader

sections.note: Human-Centered Aerospace Design & Ethics examines what changes when aerospace engineers design not only for technical performance, but also for the people, communities, and systems affected by engineering decisions. Topics include engineering failures, micro- and macroethics, human factors and ergonomics, aerospace policy, military applications, artificial intelligence, and responsible design. The course emphasizes active participation, evidence-based reasoning, respectful disagreement, and reflection rather than seminars alone. In this course, students are expected to design beyond performance and engineer for people because if the system works but the people don’t, you’re not done designing.
sections.title: Human-Centered Design & Ethics

sections.note: Introduction to CNC milling and turning using CAD/CAM software. The course will primarily focus on machining fundamentals and the manufacturing process starting at zero. The basic topics, in addition to CAM software, are speeds/feeds, tap/drill calculations, cutting tool selection, tool table/tool magazine setup, work coordinate setup, work probing, etc. The course is primarily hands-on, either CAM programming or hands-on with the machine. There is both individual and group work expected. Other than the listed prerequisite, no experience is necessary. **The course is not designed for individual and/or student group projects at this time** Prerequisite- AE 140 or equivalent CAD course Due to limited space, applications will be reviewed, and interviews will be scheduled for candidates who pass the initial round.
sections.title: Intro to Mill and Turn

sections.note: Intro to Nanosatellite Design (2hr) is a project-based course where students apply basic spacecraft mission and systems concepts to nanosatellite design through a semester long design project. Students will learn mission requirements and design processes. The course also has a lab component to introduce students to equipment and tests for simulating the space environment. Students will complete a lab training module to prepare them for potential future work in the university small satellite laboratory. This course will prepare students for ENG 491CU1 (Nanosatellite Design and Build). Students are encouraged (but not required) to take AE 298 concurrently with AE 199 Intro to Spacecraft Systems and Missions.
sections.title: Intro to Nanosatellite Design

sections.note: This class offers a collaborative international experience throughout the semester by providing an opportunity to engage with Brazilian engineering students to address an industry-driven aerospace project. Teams will be formed combining Illinois students with Brazilian students from some of their top engineering schools. At the end of the semester, the class will travel to Brazil for a series of industry visits, university-sponsored mini-projects, and cultural experiences. In addition to this project, the class will include discussions of the Brazilian aerospace industry and Brazilian culture. No experience with the Portuguese language is required (although it would be a great bonus). The trip associated with the course will be approximately 10 days and will depart within a few days after the May commencement ceremonies. Seniors are welcome in the class and on the trip (even though the trip takes place after commencement). There is a cost associated with the travel portion of the course. The course website will be hosted on Canvas. This course will count as an AE technical elective.
sections.title: Global Experience Brazil

sections.note: This course is an advanced course in the analysis and design of space structures and serves as a follow-on to Space Structures. The course will cover structural mechanics, analysis methods, and engineering considerations for spacecraft and other space structural systems, with emphasis on the relationship between structural requirements, mechanical behavior, analysis, and design. Topics may include advanced structural mechanics, spacecraft structural design and verification, structural dynamics, stability and buckling, joints and mechanisms, launch and on-orbit loading environments, and other selected topics in space structures. Advanced finite element analysis (FEA) will be integrated with analytical methods to study the behavior and performance of space structures. Selected lab experiments, computational studies, design exercises, or projects may also be incorporated to connect theoretical and numerical analysis with the behavior of physical structures. 3 credit hours for undergraduate students 4 credit hours for graduate students
sections.title: Space Structures 2

Topic: Autonomy Against the Odds: Stochastic Control for Motion and Mission Planning Stochastic control processes are often used to describe system behavior in complex, unexplored, or changing environments – the future playing fields of autonomous systems. However, performing even the simplest classical control tasks in such a framework requires the development of new theories of dynamical systems, optimal control, reachability, and adaptation. This course will serve as a gentle first introduction to that endeavor. Topics covered will include: basics of formal probability and measure theory, Markov chains, Markov decision processes, dynamic programming, optimal policies, partial observability and beliefs, robust control for uncertain processes, exploration-exploitation tradeoff and value of information, multi-agent planning, and automata and product spaces. Prerequisite: familiarity with graph theory, probability, and random variables
sections.title: Autonomy Against the Odds

sections.note: 4 credit hours. This course provides a graduate-level treatment of materials operating in severe thermal and reactive environments, with emphasis on the relationships among material composition, microstructure, processing, properties, environmental degradation, and component performance. Material systems include superalloys, refractory metals, ceramic-matrix and carbon–carbon composites, ultra-high-temperature ceramics, ablative and reusable thermal protection materials, coatings, and thermal insulators. Topics include high-temperature mechanical and thermophysical behavior, creep and thermal shock, gas–material interactions, corrosion, erosion and ablation, processing and additive manufacturing, material characterization and nondestructive evaluation, uncertainty, and material qualification. Applications are drawn from hypersonic flight, atmospheric entry, propulsion, combustion, and energy systems. Prerequisite: undergraduate thermodynamics and mechanics of materials, or equivalent preparation. Basic familiarity with heat transfer and materials science is recommended.
sections.title: High Temperature Materials

sections.note: 4 credit hours. This is a course for graduate students interested in laser-based spectroscopy and imaging of reacting and compressible flows systems. Topics include laboratory tools such as laser sources, frequency conversion, detection systems, basic optics. Background physics include review of statistical mechanics and basic molecular/atomic structure and light-matter interaction. Techniques for temperature and species measurements include Rayleigh/Raman scattering, laser-induced fluorescence, and four-wave mixing and CARS, with an emphasis on recent advancements using ultrashort-pulse fs/ps laser pulses and high-speed burst-mode systems. Methods for velocimetry in reacting flows include femtosecond molecular tagging (FLEET), four-wave mixing, filtered Rayleigh scattering, and spectroscopic approaches. This course will feature a laboratory demonstration with subsequent data analysis and reporting and two small projects. Prerequisites: Thermodynamics (ME200), Compressible Flow (AE312), Incompressible Flow (AE311) or equivalent.
sections.title: Laser & Optical Diagnostics
